what: Secure storage keeps secrets such as refresh tokens inside the phone's Keychain (iOS) or Keystore (Android), where the OS protects the keys. Biometrics (Face ID, fingerprint) add a quick check that the real owner is present before unlocking the secret or approving a sensitive action.
like: Like keeping the spare key in a hotel safe that only opens with your fingerprint, instead of under the doormat (plain storage).
why: A stolen or backed-up app file does not expose session tokens
Biometric unlock is faster than typing a password and still strong
Step-up before moving money limits damage if the phone is borrowed or the session stolen

steps.d: Capacitor Preferences replaces localStorage but is not meant as secure storage or a database. Put secrets in the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore through a plugin such as Ionic Identity Vault.
Store a refresh token, never a password or card number. Access tokens live in memory only.
On Android create a Keystore key with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true); with no validity window it needs a fresh authentication on every use.
Test isAvailable and isEnrolled, allow device PIN fallback with allowDeviceCredential, and handle USER_CANCELED, NOT_ENROLLED and lockout.
Ask for a biometric before the withdraw confirmation, then send proof to the server. A local check alone is not enough.
The backend issues a fresh short-lived step-up token or verifies a signed challenge, then approves the transfer and logs it.

choices.d: Preferences and localStorage are plain app storage and can be cleared or read from backups and compromised devices. Tokens belong in Keychain or Keystore, ideally behind a vault plugin.
A prompt that only returns true can be bypassed on a compromised device. Binding a Keystore key with a CryptoObject makes the unlock cryptographic.

choices.t: Strong only or allow device PIN
choices.d: BIOMETRIC_STRONG is the safer bar for money. Allowing the device credential improves access for users without enrolled biometrics, at lower assurance.
Once per sensitive action, such as adding a payee or confirming a withdrawal, with a short validity window for repeated actions.

instead.why: On the web, httpOnly cookies replace device secure storage
Token lifecycle, refresh and PKCE that sit above this storage layer

breaks.d: Easy to read from a backup, a rooted device or an XSS bug.
breaks.see: Stolen sessions with no login event
breaks.fix: Move to Keychain/Keystore, keep access tokens in memory

breaks.t: Biometric result trusted on the client
breaks.d: The app flips a boolean after the prompt and the API accepts every call.
breaks.fix: Bind to a Keystore key or server challenge and verify step-up proof server-side

breaks.t: New fingerprint added by an attacker
breaks.see: Access after an attacker enrols their finger
breaks.fix: Invalidate keys on biometric enrolment and force full re-login

say: Tokens live in Keychain or Keystore, never in Preferences or localStorage, and access tokens stay in memory.
Biometrics gate a Keystore-bound key and sit in front of money movement as a step-up, with PIN fallback handled.
The server verifies the step-up; the client prompt alone never authorises a transfer.

followups.a: No. It is a simple key-value store meant to replace localStorage, not a secrets vault or database. Use native secure storage for tokens.

followups.q: What if the user has no biometrics enrolled?
followups.a: Check availability and enrolment, offer device PIN where policy allows, otherwise fall back to the app login and a server-issued one-time challenge.

today: Capacitor's own security guide points teams to native Keychain and Keystore through plugins or Identity Vault rather than rolling their own. Android's BiometricPrompt with a CryptoObject is the standard way to make unlock cryptographic.

check.q: Where should a refresh token live in a hybrid app?
check.a: Keychain or Keystore via a secure plugin
d: A JS global in the bundle
check.why: Native secure storage is protected by the OS; Preferences is plain storage.

check.q: Why bind a biometric to a Keystore key?
check.a: So unlocking is cryptographic, not just a true/false result
check.why: A CryptoObject ties the prompt to a key that only works after real authentication.

check.q: Before moving money, what completes the check?
check.a: The server verifies a step-up proof
check.why: Client checks can be bypassed, so the backend decides.
